en: To leave quickly and secretly, often to escape arrest or with stolen money
hook: ABS-COND: ABSent with the CONDominium money.
story: Abscond. For five years, the treasurer of a village savings group in Mymensingh collected deposits from two hundred families. One morning his house was empty and the safe stood open. A bus conductor remembered a man with a heavy bag buying a ticket to the border. He had absconded: left quickly and secretly, taking the money. The word comes from the Latin for to hide away. Prisoners abscond from jail; cashiers abscond with funds. Synonyms: flee, bolt, decamp.

gre.s: Days before the auditors arrived, the firm's accountant chose to ____ with millions in client funds, slipping out of the country under a false name.
gre.clue: slipping out of the country under a false name

en: The highest or most successful point; the point in an orbit farthest from Earth
hook: APO-GEE: AWAY (apo) from Earth (geo), the farthest, highest point.
story: Apogee. Tanvir's grandfather was a village jatra actor. The apogee of his career came in 1985, when he performed before ten thousand people at a festival in Dhaka. After that, the crowds slowly shrank. An apogee is the highest or most successful point. In astronomy, it is the point in the orbit of the Moon or a satellite farthest from Earth: apo means away, and gee means earth. Its opposite is perigee. Synonyms: peak, zenith, pinnacle.

gre.s: Critics agree that the novelist's career reached its ____ with her third book; nothing she wrote afterward came close to its brilliance or its success.
gre.clue: nothing she wrote afterward came close

en: An attack on someone's reputation or character
hook: ASPERSION: SPRINKLING dirt on someone's name.
story: Aspersion. Before the student union election, anonymous posters appeared around campus claiming that Sara, the leading candidate, had bought her grades and stolen club funds. None of it was true, but some voters believed it. Her rivals were casting aspersions on her: attacking her reputation and character. The usual phrase is cast aspersions. Originally, aspersion meant sprinkling water, so picture someone spattering mud on your good name. Synonyms: slur, slander, smear.

gre.s: Unable to fault the research itself, her rivals resorted to an anonymous ____ on her character, hinting at plagiarism they could never prove.
gre.clue: hinting at plagiarism they could never prove

en: Humorously rude and indecent
hook: BAWDY: BAWLING out rude jokes.
story: Bawdy. At village weddings in the old days, women from the groom's side would sing teasing songs full of jokes about married life, making the bride blush and the aunties roar with laughter. The songs were bawdy: humorously rude and indecent. Bawdy humour is crude but cheerful, not cruel. Shakespeare's plays are full of bawdy puns that schoolbooks quietly skip. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: ribald, racy, risque.

gre.s: The comedian's ____ jokes, full of sexual innuendo, delighted the late-night crowd but would never have been permitted on family television.
gre.clue: full of sexual innuendo

en: Annoyance or distress caused by humiliation or failure
hook: CHAGRIN: you wanted to GRIN, but SHAME (cha) took over.
story: Chagrin. Farhan told all his friends that he would top the class in the final exam. When the results came out, he had failed one subject, and his quiet roommate had come first. Farhan's face burned with chagrin: annoyance and distress caused by humiliation or failure. It often appears as, much to his chagrin. Chagrin is not plain sadness; it is the sting of embarrassment. Despite the sound, there is no grin in it. Synonyms: mortification, vexation.

gre.s: Much to the general's ____, the battle he had boasted would last a single afternoon dragged on for months, exposing his strategy as hopelessly naive.
gre.clue: he had boasted would last a single afternoon

en: To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose
hook: COL-LUDE: playing (ludere) together secretly.
story: Collude. Three cement companies in one city met in secret and agreed to raise their prices together, so builders had no cheaper option. The government later fined them all. They had colluded: cooperated secretly for a dishonest purpose. The noun is collusion. Students who share answers during an online exam are colluding too. Col means together and ludere means to play, so to collude is to play together, but in a crooked game. Synonyms: conspire, connive, scheme.

gre.s: Investigators suspected that the two rival bidders had secretly agreed to ____, inflating their offers so that the government would pay far more than the project was worth.
gre.clue: secretly agreed

en: To express sympathy or sorrow
hook: COM-MISERATE: share someone's MISERY.
story: Commiserate. After the exam results came out, Rumana and her friends sat on the hostel roof. Three of them had failed the same difficult course. They shared tea, complained about the impossible questions, and comforted one another until midnight. They were commiserating: expressing sympathy and sorrow for each other. Com means with, and miser means wretched, as in misery, so to commiserate is to share someone's misery. Synonyms: sympathize, console, condole.

gre.s: When the factory closed, former coworkers gathered every evening at the tea stall to ____ with one another over lost wages and uncertain futures.
gre.clue: over lost wages and uncertain futures

en: A large, destructive fire
hook: CONFLAGRATION: a FLAG-burning FLAME everywhere.
story: Conflagration. One night, a fire broke out in a chemical warehouse in Old Dhaka. Flames leapt from building to building through the narrow lanes, gas cylinders exploded, and firefighters battled for hours. By morning, whole blocks had turned to ash. It was a conflagration: a large, destructive fire. Con means together and flagrare means to burn, the root of flagrant. The word can also describe a war that spreads like fire. Synonyms: inferno, blaze, firestorm.

gre.s: What began as a small kitchen fire soon became a ____ that consumed half the town, as dry winds drove the flames from roof to roof.
gre.clue: consumed half the town

en: An unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute
hook: CONTRE-TEMPS: French for 'against time' — bad timing.
story: Contretemps. At Joya's engagement ceremony, the groom's mother arrived wearing exactly the same sari as the bride's mother. There was an awkward silence, a few stiff smiles, and then a short argument about who should change. The family still laughs about that contretemps: an unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute. The word is French, meaning against the time, and is pronounced KON-truh-tahn. Synonyms: mishap, hitch, squabble.

gre.s: The diplomats' brief ____ over seating arrangements, though embarrassing at the time, was soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations that followed.
gre.clue: soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations

en: A firmly held belief; also, a formal declaration of guilt
hook: CONVICTION: you're CONVINCED.
story: Conviction. Tania's grandmother was the first woman in her village to send her daughters to college. Neighbours mocked her, relatives warned her, and money was always short. But she never wavered; she was certain that education would change her family. She acted from deep conviction: a firmly held belief. The word has a second meaning, a formal declaration that someone is guilty of a crime. Convict and convince share its root. Synonyms: belief, certainty, resolve.

gre.s: Though the young activist spoke softly, she argued with such ____ that even her skeptical audience could not doubt she believed every word.
gre.clue: could not doubt she believed every word

en: To sing or hum softly and sentimentally
hook: CROON: like a CROONER singing softly into the moon.
story: Croon. Late at night on the river, an old boatman rows slowly and croons a bhatiali song, soft and low, his voice drifting across the dark water. In a house on the bank, Kamal's mother croons a lullaby until the baby falls asleep. To croon is to sing or hum softly and sentimentally. In the 1940s, smooth, gentle singers like Frank Sinatra were called crooners. Think of a voice that coos rather than shouts. Synonyms: hum, warble, murmur.

gre.s: Rather than belting out the song as most performers did, he chose to ____ it softly, turning the rousing anthem into an intimate lullaby.
gre.clue: Rather than belting out the song

en: To remove from power suddenly and forcefully
hook: DE-POSE: remove from the throne POSITION.
story: Depose. In 1757, Siraj ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab of Bengal, lost the Battle of Plassey because his own commander, Mir Jafar, secretly sided with the British. Siraj was deposed: removed from power suddenly and forcefully. Mir Jafar took his throne, and in Bengal his name still means traitor. In law, depose has another sense, to question a witness under oath. De means down, and pose means to put: to put down. Synonyms: overthrow, oust, topple.

gre.s: Fearing that the increasingly erratic king would ruin the nation, his generals plotted to ____ him and install his young nephew on the throne.
gre.clue: install his young nephew on the throne

en: The easing of hostility between countries
hook: DETENTE: like DE-TENSE, reducing tension.
story: Detente. During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union aimed thousands of nuclear missiles at each other. In the 1970s, their leaders began signing arms agreements, trading grain, and even flying a joint space mission. That period of relaxed tension was called detente: the easing of hostility between countries. Detente is French for loosening, like releasing a tightly drawn bowstring. Its opposite is escalation. Synonyms: rapprochement, thaw.

gre.s: After decades of border skirmishes, the two neighbors entered a period of ____, reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors for the first time in a generation.
gre.clue: reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors

en: Dull and unfashionable in appearance
hook: DOWDY: DULL and DOWNbeat style.
story: Dowdy. At the office's annual party, everyone arrived in bright new outfits. Mitu's aunt appeared in a faded brown dress decades out of style, with a shapeless grey cardigan on top. A few colleagues whispered that she looked dowdy: dull and unfashionable in appearance. She did not care; she danced more than anyone. The word can describe places too, like a dowdy hotel with tired carpets. Its opposite is chic. Synonyms: frumpy, drab, unfashionable.

gre.s: Once dismissed as ____, with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture, the old hotel was transformed by its new owners into the most stylish address in the city.
gre.clue: with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture

en: A level or rank in an organization or society
hook: ECHELON: like the steps of a LADDER, rung by rung.
story: Echelon. In a large bank, tellers and clerks work at the bottom, managers in the middle, and a few directors at the very top make the big decisions. Each level is an echelon: a level or rank in an organization or society. People often speak of the upper echelons of power. The word comes from the French for a rung of a ladder. In the army, an echelon is also a formation of troops arranged like steps. Synonyms: rank, tier, level.

gre.s: Although she began as a junior typist, her talent eventually carried her to the highest ____ of the company, where she helped set policy for thousands of employees.
gre.clue: Although she began as a junior typist

en: A feeling of weariness and dissatisfaction from lack of interest
hook: ENNUI (on-WEE): French for boredom. 'Oh, wee, another day.'
story: Ennui. During the long summer break, Lamia had nothing to do. She scrolled her phone, napped, stared at the ceiling fan, and sighed. Even her favourite films felt dull. It was not sadness exactly, but a heavy, restless weariness. That feeling is ennui. Say it on-WEE. It is French, and related to the English word annoy. Ennui is deeper than ordinary boredom; it is a listless dissatisfaction with life itself. Synonyms: listlessness, tedium, languor.

gre.s: Wealthy beyond need and freed from any obligation to work, the aristocrats of the novel suffer from a pervasive ____, drifting from party to party without interest or purpose.
gre.clue: drifting from party to party without interest or purpose

en: To speak or write at great length
hook: EX-PATIATE: wander out (spatiari) in long speech.
story: Expatiate. Ask Professor Kabir a simple question about the weather, and he will expatiate on monsoon patterns, rainfall records since British times, climate change, and a rain poem by Jibanananda Das. Forty minutes later, you will still be standing there. To expatiate is to speak or write at great length. It comes from the Latin for wandering widely. Do not confuse it with expiate, to atone, or expatriate, to leave one's country. Synonyms: elaborate, expound, dilate.

gre.s: Given just five minutes at the conference, the speaker could not ____ on her research as she had hoped, and offered only a brief summary of her findings.
gre.clue: offered only a brief summary of her findings

en: Filled with something undesirable; causing anxiety
hook: FRAUGHT: FREIGHT-loaded with danger.
story: Fraught. The night before the final match, the dressing room was fraught with tension. Two players had quarrelled, the captain was injured, and the coach's job depended on the result. Nobody slept. Fraught means filled with something undesirable, such as danger, tension or difficulty, and it is often followed by with. Used alone, it means causing anxiety, as in a fraught conversation. It shares a root with freight: heavily loaded. Synonyms: laden, tense, charged.

gre.s: The negotiations were ____ with danger from the start: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war that had only just ended.
gre.clue: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war

en: The support on which a lever pivots; a central or essential element
hook: FULCRUM: the PIVOT point of a seesaw.
story: Fulcrum. On a playground seesaw, the plank rests on a single support in the middle. That support is the fulcrum: the point on which a lever pivots. Archimedes boasted that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the Earth. Figuratively, a fulcrum is a central or essential element. In Rafi's family, his grandmother is the fulcrum; every big decision turns on her. Synonyms: pivot, linchpin, crux.

gre.s: As the only member trusted by both factions, the young senator became the ____ of the negotiations, the point around which every compromise turned.
gre.clue: the point around which every compromise turned

en: An extremely confused, complicated, or embarrassing situation
hook: IMBROGLIO: an EMBROIDERY of tangled threads.
story: Imbroglio. It began with a forwarded message in a family group chat. One cousin misread it as an insult, an aunt took sides, two uncles stopped speaking, a wedding invitation was withdrawn, and somehow an old land dispute was revived. Nobody remembered the original message. It was an imbroglio: an extremely confused, complicated or embarrassing situation. The word is Italian, related to embroil, to tangle someone up. Synonyms: entanglement, muddle, mess.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error grew into a diplomatic ____ involving three governments, two banks, and a tangle of contradictory lawsuits.
gre.clue: a tangle of contradictory lawsuits

en: Cheerful and lighthearted
hook: JOCUND: JOKING and JOLLY.
story: Jocund. Every year on Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, Dhaka fills with jocund crowds. People in red and white laugh, sing, eat panta bhat with hilsa, and dance to the drums. Even strangers smile at one another. The mood is jocund: cheerful and lighthearted. It comes from the Latin for pleasant, influenced by the Latin word for joke. Wordsworth wrote of the jocund company of daffodils. Synonyms: merry, jovial, cheerful.

gre.s: The mood at the reunion was ____, with old friends laughing and singing late into the night, utterly unlike the somber gathering the organizers had feared.
gre.clue: laughing and singing late into the night

en: To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation
bn: দুর্বল হয়ে পড়া; কষ্টে দিন কাটানো
hook: LANGUISH: become LANGUID, weak and fading.
story: Languish. A young activist was arrested and held without trial. Months turned into years. In a cramped cell he grew thin and pale, while his case file gathered dust in a government office. He languished in prison: he suffered in an unpleasant situation and slowly lost strength. Plants languish without water; projects languish without funding. Languish shares a root with languid, meaning weak and slow. Synonyms: wither, decline, waste away.

gre.s: Without fresh investment, the once thriving port continued to ____, its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling into the harbor.
gre.clue: its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling

en: The lowest point
hook: NADIR: the opposite of zenith, the bottom of everything.
story: Nadir. The year Arif's father lost his business, the family sold their car, moved into a single rented room, and Arif nearly dropped out of school. That winter was the nadir of their lives: the lowest point. Slowly, things improved. In astronomy, the nadir is the point directly below an observer, opposite the zenith overhead. Both words come from Arabic. Remember: nadir is down, zenith is up. Synonyms: low point, rock bottom.

gre.s: The team's season reached its ____ in March, when a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place; only then did its slow recovery begin.
gre.clue: a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place

en: Quick and light in movement; quick-thinking
hook: NIMBLE: as quick as a NIMBLE squirrel.
story: Nimble. In the crowded Gulistan market, a young porter carries a basket of vegetables on his head, weaving between rickshaws, buses and shoppers without ever bumping anyone. His feet are nimble: quick and light in movement. Nimble also describes the mind, so a nimble debater answers tricky questions instantly. Remember the nursery rhyme: Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick. Synonyms: agile, deft, spry.

gre.s: Though the old pianist's body had grown frail, his fingers remained astonishingly ____, racing through the most difficult passages without a single error.
gre.clue: racing through the most difficult passages

en: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen
hook: OMINOUS: an OMEN of bad things.
story: Ominous. Fishermen at Cox's Bazar noticed the sky turning a strange copper colour. The wind died, the birds disappeared, and the sea went flat and silent. The old men pulled their boats high up the beach. The signs were ominous: they suggested that something bad was about to happen. That night, the cyclone arrived. Ominous comes from omen, a sign of what the future holds. Synonyms: menacing, foreboding, sinister.

gre.s: The doctors' sudden silence and averted eyes were ____, and the family braced themselves for bad news before a single word was spoken.
gre.clue: braced themselves for bad news

en: Bizarrely strange or unusual
hook: OUT-LANDISH: from an OUTside LAND, totally foreign and weird.
story: Outlandish. Sabbir arrived at his cousin's wedding wearing a purple suit covered in silver stars, green shoes, and a hat shaped like a fish. The aunties gasped, the children giggled, and the photographer could not stop laughing. His outfit was outlandish: bizarrely strange and unusual. An outlandish claim is one so strange it is hard to believe. Originally the word meant foreign, from out land, another country. Synonyms: bizarre, weird, preposterous.

gre.s: The theory that the pyramids were built by visitors from another planet is so ____ that serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it.
gre.clue: serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it

en: Favorable; indicating a good chance of success
hook: PROPITIOUS: PROPER time to act — the signs are favorable.
story: Propitious. Farmers in Rangpur waited anxiously for the planting season. Then the rains arrived on time, the soil was soft, fertiliser prices fell, and new seeds came from the research institute. Everything pointed to a good harvest. The conditions were propitious: favourable, indicating a good chance of success. Propitious comes from the Latin for gracious, as if the gods were smiling on you. Its close cousin is auspicious. Synonyms: favourable, opportune, promising.

gre.s: Investors were wary of launching the venture during a recession, but the sudden drop in interest rates made the moment unexpectedly ____.
gre.clue: the sudden drop in interest rates

en: Having or encouraging an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters
hook: PRURIENT: like an ITCH (prurire = to itch) for scandal.
story: Prurient. When a famous actor was hospitalized, some tabloids printed almost nothing about his health. Instead, they ran pages of gossip about his secret romances, with blurry photos taken through windows. Readers bought every copy. The tabloids fed a prurient interest: an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters. Prurient comes from the Latin for itching, so think of an itch for scandal. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: lewd, salacious, voyeuristic.

gre.s: Critics charged that the documentary, despite its claims to serious journalism, merely catered to viewers' ____ curiosity, lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs.
gre.clue: lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs

en: Taking pleasure in causing pain or suffering to others
hook: SADISTIC: makes others SAD and enjoys it.
story: Sadistic. In an old prison film, a guard forces the prisoners to stand in the burning sun for hours, then laughs as they faint, and smiles while ordering more punishment. He enjoys their pain. He is sadistic: taking pleasure in causing pain or suffering to others. The word comes from the Marquis de Sade, an eighteenth-century French writer notorious for cruelty in his novels. Students sometimes joke that a brutal exam is sadistic. Synonyms: cruel, vicious, barbarous.

gre.s: The guard was not merely strict but ____, devising humiliating punishments for minor offenses and visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering.
gre.clue: visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering

en: The highest point; the peak of success
hook: ZENITH: the sun straight overhead, the top of the sky.
story: Zenith. Mughal power reached its zenith in the seventeenth century, when the empire stretched across most of the subcontinent and Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal. After that, it slowly declined. The zenith is the highest point, the peak of success. In astronomy, it is the point in the sky directly above an observer. Remember: zenith is up, nadir is down. Both came into English from Arabic astronomy. Synonyms: peak, pinnacle, apex.

gre.s: At the ____ of his fame, the singer could fill any stadium in the country; a decade later, he was performing in near-empty halls.
gre.clue: could fill any stadium in the country
